notes: The edited volume is a guild-revisionist intervention; it does not prove that guilds were uniformly innovative or optimal.
Rules must be distinguished from enforcement and everyday practice.
The case geography is concentrated in central and western Europe and the volume lacks a sustained gender analysis.
Knowledge-emergence labels such as the skill-mobility-diffusion triad are routing hypotheses, not quotations from the book.
Clean text was spot-checked only; archival references and quantitative claims remain unverified.
original_spot_checks: clean lines 57-80: the introduction identifies apprenticeship, subcontracting, labor mobility and tacit knowledge as mechanisms.
clean lines 103-132: apprenticeship attrition, family training and subcontracting complicate a single formal model.
clean lines 150-165: tacit knowledge, collective sharing and resistance to private monopoly are separated.
clean lines 189-226: guild responses to technology are conditional and Ogilvie's rent-seeking counterexample is retained.
clean lines 258-262: the editors deny that guilds were an optimal or universally growth-promoting solution.
